title: I/O methods and multiprocessors
subtitle: Three ways to talk to a device, and how many processors are connected and kept in agreement.

prog.title: Programmed I/O
prog.body: With programmed I/O the CPU issues a command and then polls the device’s status register until it is ready, then moves the data itself. It is simple but wastes the CPU: a keyboard polled at full speed spends virtually all its time looking at nothing.

int.title: Interrupt-driven I/O
int.body: The CPU starts the operation and goes on running other instructions. When the device is ready it raises an interrupt; the CPU finishes its current instruction, saves state, runs a service routine that moves the word, and returns. Efficiency is much better, but every word still costs an interrupt — too expensive for disks.

dma.title: Direct memory access
dma.body: A DMA controller is given the memory address, the count and the direction, then transfers the whole block between device and memory by itself, stealing bus cycles ("cycle stealing") from the CPU, and interrupts once at the end. One interrupt per block instead of one per word.
dma.steps: Transfer a 4 KB block from a device that gives one 4-byte word per transfer. Interrupt-driven: one interrupt per word. DMA: one interrupt per block.

chan.title: Channels and interfaces
chan.body: An I/O channel is a small processor that runs its own I/O program, freeing the CPU further (mainframes); a front-end processor does the same for communications. External interfaces are point-to-point (USB, SATA) or multipoint buses (SCSI): serial links are replacing wide parallel ones because they scale in speed.

mp.title: Multiprocessors and interconnection
mp.body: A tightly-coupled multiprocessor shares memory. Processors are joined by a time-shared common bus (cheap, one at a time), multiport memory, a crossbar switch (any processor to any memory, n² crosspoints), a multistage network (log₂ n stages of small switches) or a hypercube (n = 2ᵈ nodes, each with d neighbours). Arbitration decides who wins a contested resource.
mp.steps: Crossbar for 8 processors and 8 memories needs 8 × 8 crosspoints. An omega network needs (n/2) log₂ n 2×2 switches.

summary.title: Summary
summary.body:
• Polling wastes CPU; interrupts free it; DMA moves whole blocks with one interrupt.
  • Interconnect choice trades cost against simultaneous transfers.
